column3: Exact reprise of commanded entry through Hell's gates, permanent residence, and the evil abode of the arrogant.
Its entry into Yusuf's shelter and relief from distress only faintly contrasts with the focus's punitive entry.
A peaceful, enduring entry provides a clear positive counterpart to the focus's irreversible punitive threshold.
It exactly repeats the formula, but adds little after the fuller exact parallel at 39:72.
The same-surah portrait of the sealed arrogant heart supplies a proximate cause for the focus's final abode.
It explicitly makes the Fire a lasting abode, clarifying how chosen alliances end in fixed residence.
Hell and an evil resting place reinforce the punitive destination, though without gates, permanence, or arrogance.
A refused earthly entry at a gate offers only a distant contrast to compelled entry in the focus.
Heavenly gates open for flooding, a different controlled-threshold image with little bearing on the focus's verdict.
It joins Hell as an abode to the arrogant, but is less direct than the exact formula already reviewed.
The same surah directly states that those too arrogant for worship will enter Hell humbled.
Garden entry through every gate supplies a broad positive counter-image, now redundant after earlier entry contrasts.
It confirms lasting residence in the Fire and an evil final destination, without the focus's gate or arrogance frame.
Its commanded crossing of a gate into victory contrasts only loosely with the condemned entry of the focus.
A hypothetical heavenly opening concerns persistent denial of signs rather than the focus's final residence.
An evil place of settlement among the condemned supports the tone but adds no focused entry or permanence relation.
The same-surah bad abode for wrongdoers gives nearby consequence context without the focus's threshold language.
The question of admission to a blissful garden is a broad inverse of the focus's commanded admission to Hell.
Enduring garden admission is a generic positive counterpart and adds little after 50:34 and 13:23.
Safe family entry into Egypt is a different shelter scene with no punitive-residence connection.
Obedience leading to garden admission gives a general alternative outcome, not a clarification of the focus.
It names Hell as an abode for deniers, adding the truth-rejection ground for a fixed punitive residence.
The same-surah stages of creation and death give remote context but do not clarify the gates or permanent abode.
It directly states that criminals remain in Hell's punishment, reinforcing the focus's permanence.
Multiple earthly gates and reliance on God concern prudent travel, not the one-way punitive threshold.
Building for imagined permanence is a distant human counterpoint to the actual permanence announced in the focus.
It confirms that Fire-dwellers remain there, but repeats an already well-covered consequence.
Joyful garden entry with spouses is a broad positive contrast, not a close aid to the focus.
Recognition at Yusuf's court has no material relation to gates, Hell, or lasting residence.
A gate entered in humility for forgiveness provides a distant moral inverse of the arrogant's destination.
It names Hell as the abode of those who reject truth, supplying another causal frame for the focus's residence.
A pleasing entrance for the displaced contrasts broadly with the focus's unwelcome entry.
The path of Hell and everlasting residence closely support the focus's one-way destination.
Arrogance closes heavenly gates and bars garden entry, directly opposing the focus's forced opening into Hell.
Entry into mercy for believers is a generic positive alternative already represented by stronger contrasts.
Its duration language is broad and lacks the focus's Hell, gate, and arrogance nexus.
Hell as an evil destination follows secret sin, but adds little to the focus's specific final formula.
Honorable lodging for Yusuf is too different from the focus's punitive abode.
Enduring a burden at resurrection loosely supports permanence but not the focus's particular residence.
A bad companion at final arrival does not clarify entry through Hell's gates or its duration.
Recognized garden entry is a broad inverse with little marginal value.
Movement from darkness to light and enduring garden entry offer a general positive alternative only.
Entering wholly into peace is not a focused parallel to the condemned entry in the focus.
The Fire as an abode from which no restored acceptance follows sharply reinforces irreversible punitive residence.
Everlasting gardens are a generic positive counterpart and are redundant in this list.
The command to enter the garden in peace contrasts with the focus but adds no new structural detail.
It explicitly calls the Fire their house of permanence, strongly supporting the focus's lasting abode.
Entry into mercy after rescue is only a broad opposite movement.
Enduring good dwellings for believers form a generic positive contrast to the focus's evil dwelling.
The prayer for truthful entry and exit contrasts conceptually with the focus's one-way forced entrance.
Permanent youthful attendants do not clarify the focus's permanent punitive residence.
Successive communities are commanded into the Fire, adding collective entry and mutual condemnation within it.
Garden admission is another generic positive counterpart with little added value.
Forgiveness followed by garden admission gives only a distant inverse outcome.
It directly fixes wrongdoers together in the Fire forever, reinforcing the focus's permanence.
The command to enter the holy land contrasts with the focus only at the level of commanded entry.
Permanent attendants around the blessed have no focused relation to the condemned abode.
Hell as a refuge with no escape directly reinforces the focus's irreversible residence.
The command to taste everlasting punishment makes the focus's lasting abode an ongoing punitive condition.
Disobedience ends in everlasting Hell, directly confirming permanent punitive confinement.
It explicitly promises hypocrites and disbelievers enduring Hell and a lasting punishment.
Being put into the Fire is public disgrace without helpers, sharpening the focus's humiliation of the arrogant.
Unsupported claims to garden admission are only a remote contrast to the focus's sentence.
It states that disbelievers remain forever in Hell, reinforcing the permanent outcome.
Mutual patronage among wrongdoers gives background to 6:128 but does not itself clarify the focus.
A covenantal command to enter a gate in prostration is a distant inverse of the arrogant's entry.
Unrelieved punishment and no reprieve make the focus's permanent abode explicitly inescapable.
The punishment is not eased, reinforcing the focus's enduring adverse residence.
Entry into mercy through forgiveness is a broad positive inverse with limited marginal value.
Being carried from drowning into Fire depicts compelled transfer into punishment, though not lasting residence.
Gate opening, custodial greeting, and permanent entry into the garden provide a structured positive counterpart.
Garden entry after trial gives a remote positive alternative rather than explaining the focus.
Everlasting, unrelieved punishment clearly reinforces the permanence of the focus's abode.
Secure entry into the Sacred Mosque is a different authorized-threshold scene.
Inclusion among the righteous has only a general inverse relation to the focus's exclusion.
Hell and an evil resting place reiterate the destination but add no new focused element.
The Book's revelation from the Mighty, Wise does not clarify the focus's entry or residence.
Garden admission for believers is a generic positive contrast already covered repeatedly.
Prepared enduring gardens provide little beyond the existing positive counter-images.
Inheritance alone does not clarify the focus without the following verse's lasting residence.
House doors and couches describe worldly ornament, not the focus's punitive threshold.
The command to remain in the Fire and cease speech makes the enclosure's finality explicit.
Enduring inherited Paradise is a generic positive counter-image.
The Fire-dweller's permanence follows a specific economic prohibition and adds little to the focus.
Enduring garden residence without seeking change is a broad positive inverse.
Just garden entry for believing righteous people is a generic alternative outcome.
The Fire-dwellers' permanence is attached to a light-darkness contrast, only loosely aiding the focus.
A good lasting place of settlement is a broad positive contrast, now redundant.
The call to enter dwellings for protection is a different, temporary shelter threshold.
Repentance, faith, and righteous action leading to garden entry supply only a general alternative.
The unjust are left kneeling there after the God-fearing are rescued, clarifying selective permanence in punishment.
Loss of the self results in permanent Hell, reinforcing the focus's settled punitive outcome.
The declaration that Hell will be filled gives a collective consequence but not entry or lasting residence.
Enduring garden companionship is a generic positive inverse with little marginal value.
The absence of vain speech in a garden does not illuminate the focus's Hell formula.
Authorized, time-limited household entry contrasts only distantly with the focus's permanent compelled entry.
Finding one Muslim household has no focused relation to the condemned abode.
Entry into mercy amid protected people is a distant positive admission scene.
Severe punishment for disbelievers supplies only a broad consequence already established.
The honored guests of Abraham do not clarify the focus's gates, Hell, or permanence.
The immediate prelude binds the condemned in shackles before the gates-and-abiding verdict of the focus.
It traces the bound group from boiling water into the Fire, supplying the coercive approach to the focus's entry.
It continues the transfer by placing them into the Fire, directly preceding the focus's gate command.
Their failed invocation of associates exposes the abandonment that culminates in the focus's permanent abode.
It names wrongful exultation and insolence as the moral ground immediately before the focus's address to the arrogant.
It supplies the procession, opened gates, keepers, and command sequence whose final formula is stated at 39:72.
The wish to leave the Fire and the declaration that they will not leave it directly clarify the focus's irreversible residence.
Arrogance before the signs closes the gates of heaven and bars garden entry, directly opposing the focus's entry through Hell's gates.
It explicitly makes deniers and the arrogant companions of the Fire abiding therein.
Hell as bedding and covering gives the focus's abode an enclosing, inescapable form.
It identifies the Fire as the abode earned by what people acquired, supplying a consequence frame for the focus.
It names the Fire-dwellers as abiding therein, reinforcing the focus's permanent residence.
Chains, the Fire, and everlasting residence join restraint to the focus's enduring punitive destination.
Fire lies ahead of the tyrant, extending the focus's condemnation of arrogance into its assigned destination.
The inability to die while punishment comes from every side sharpens the focus's irreversible confinement.
Gathering on faces and an ever-renewed Hell abode make the punitive destination explicitly enduring.
The Fire encloses its people and offers no relieving response, clarifying the hostile character of the focus's abode.
The guilty see the Fire, know they will fall into it, and find no turning away, closely matching one-way entry.
The criminal's Fire contains neither death nor life, making the focus's permanence an unending punitive condition.
The coming Fire that cannot be turned from faces and backs reinforces the unavoidable arrival at punishment.
It begins the Fire scene with garments of fire and poured boiling liquid, detailing the punishment behind the focus's residence.
Every attempt to leave the Fire is returned to it, directly defining the focus's one-way boundary.
Fire scorches faces within it, supplying the bodily condition of those fixed in the focus's abode.
The inmates confess their misguidance and being overcome, adding their own recognition within the Fire scene.
Their plea to be brought out is answered by the following command to remain, directly delimiting escape from the focus's abode.
Being cast bound into a narrow place in Hell supplies a confined form of the focus's lasting entry.
The prohibition on seeking a single destruction reinforces punishment that cannot be terminated by one ending.
Hell is named an evil settlement and residence, closely echoing the focus's evil abode.
Its evil settlement and station directly parallels the focus's evaluation of the lasting abode.
Whenever the wicked seek to leave the Fire they are returned to it, directly clarifying irreversible residence.
The cursed are assigned a blazing Fire, providing the punitive verdict behind the focus's command.
Their eternal stay in the Fire without protector or helper reinforces the focus's permanent abandonment.
The Fire-dwellers neither die nor receive eased punishment, directly amplifying permanent confinement.
The direct identification of Hell as the promised destination supports the focus's final command of entry.
Their return is to the blazing Fire, reinforcing a destination that admits no settled alternative.
It announces an evil return for transgressors immediately before Hell is named as their bed.
The Fire becomes their shelter after forgetting the meeting, reinforcing a final residence with no exit.
The command to cast every stubborn denier into Hell closely parallels the focus's commanded placement.
The sentence to cast the obstinate associate-maker into severe punishment reinforces the focus's coercive verdict.
The condemned are thrust into the Fire, adding a forceful entry image to the focus's threshold command.
The demand to endure the Fire without distinction between patience and impatience reinforces unavoidable punishment.
Dragging people on their faces into the Fire supplies a concrete compelled-entry counterpart.
It identifies Hell as the reality denied by the guilty, directly framing the focus's destination.
Circling between Hell and boiling water expands the punitive environment of the focus's abode.
The companions of the left introduce the opposed final class that culminates in the Fire scene.
Scorching wind and boiling water detail the adverse environment corresponding to the focus's evil abode.
The Fire is declared their proper refuge, closely supporting the focus's fixed abode language.
The guarded Fire and its stern custodians clarify the controlled gates and custodial setting of the focus.
Those who disbelieve have the punishment of Hell and an evil destination, closely echoing the focus's final evaluation.
The command to seize and shackle the condemned supplies the restraint before punitive confinement.
The command to burn him in Hell directly parallels the focus's imperative sentence.
The blazing Fire is introduced as the inescapable contrary answer to attempted ransom.
The divine declaration of entry into Saqar supplies another direct sentence of punitive admission.
The specified guardians of Saqar reinforce the guarded, controlled entry motif of the focus.
Hell is set as a place of ambush, clarifying the prepared destination awaiting transgressors.
Remaining there for ages makes the prepared Hell destination durationally fixed.
The wicked are explicitly in Hell, reinforcing the final placement without further threshold detail.
Calling for a blaze names the Fire as the consequence following the final record and reckoning.
Entering a scorching Fire supplies a concise direct counterpart to the focus's entry command.
The abyss as the final home gives another compact formulation of a punitive settled destination.
The command to cast the slanderer into the Crusher parallels the focus's imperative entry into Hell.
The Fire is closed over them, making permanent enclosure explicit.
The announced entry into a blazing Fire gives a direct but less developed punitive-admission parallel.
